lesson.title: Five Shots on King Street: The Boston Massacre
lesson.summary: On a cold March night in 1770, a street confrontation between British soldiers and a Boston crowd ended in gunfire, leaving five colonists dead and giving Patriot leaders a powerful symbol of British tyranny.
lesson.body:
By 1768 Britain had stationed roughly two thousand soldiers in Boston to enforce the customs duties created by the Townshend Acts and to keep order in a city that had grown openly hostile to Parliament's tax laws. Boston at the time had a population of only about sixteen thousand people, so the presence of so many redcoats felt like an occupation to many residents. Off duty soldiers also took part time jobs to supplement their low pay, which put them in direct competition with local laborers, ropemakers, and dockworkers. That daily friction, layered on top of years of anger over taxation without representation, made Boston a tinderbox by the start of 1770, with small scuffles between soldiers and townspeople breaking out for weeks before the final crisis.

On the evening of March 5, 1770, a crowd gathered near the Custom House on King Street and began taunting a lone British sentry, Private Hugh White, throwing snowballs, chunks of ice, and oyster shells. As the mob grew larger and louder, Captain Thomas Preston led a small detachment of soldiers to support White. In the chaos and shouting, someone gave an order, or perhaps only shouted the word fire, and the soldiers began shooting into the crowd. Exactly who gave the command, and whether one was given at all, remains disputed to this day, and it became the central legal question at the soldiers' later trial.

Five colonists died from the gunfire, either that night or in the days that followed. Crispus Attucks, a dockworker of African and Native American ancestry, is often remembered as the first person killed in the cause of American independence. He died alongside Samuel Gray, James Caldwell, Samuel Maverick, and Patrick Carr, who succumbed to his wounds about two weeks later. Several other colonists were wounded in the volley.

Samuel Adams and other Patriot leaders moved quickly to publicize the killings, and Paul Revere produced a widely circulated engraving that depicted the soldiers as a firing line coolly gunning down unarmed civilians. The image was more propaganda than accurate reporting, but it spread through the colonies and helped fix the label Boston Massacre in the public imagination, turning a chaotic street brawl into a symbol of British military tyranny. For years afterward, Bostonians held public commemorations each March 5 to keep the memory of the dead alive.

What happened next revealed a different side of the colonial response. John Adams, though a committed Patriot, agreed to defend Captain Preston and the soldiers at trial, joined by fellow lawyer Josiah Quincy, because he believed every accused person deserved a fair defense under the law. Most of the soldiers were acquitted, and two were convicted only of manslaughter and branded on the thumb. Adams later regarded this unpopular defense as one of the most important services of his career.

The massacre grew directly out of the resentment the Townshend Acts had created by placing British troops in Boston to enforce customs duties in the first place. Without that military presence, there would have been no soldiers on King Street to clash with the crowd. The episode hardened colonial opinion against standing armies stationed among civilians and became one more grievance Patriot leaders pointed to in the years leading up to the Boston Tea Party.
